narrative:
The model estimated a 72.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was denied because the admissions decision treated that risk as too high. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it was strong enough to drive rejection.

The strongest factor pushing toward failure was your third-year class standing: your third-year decile was 1, far below the accepted-student average of about 5.8. The next most important factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 39 was above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so this actually pushed toward passing and worked in your favor. The third most influential factor was your first-year class standing: your first-year decile was 2, compared with an accepted-student average of 6, and this also pushed toward failure. In short, two academic-standing signals were the main reasons for denial, while your LSAT partly offset that concern. Your gender and race were not used in this decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record, especially through consistently strong upper-level coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, and ask admissions offices whether updated grades can be considered. Seek admissions counseling, document any relevant circumstances, and consider delaying reapplication until you can show clear academic improvement. Retake the LSAT only if practice tests suggest meaningful gains.
